> Which leads me to three questions:
> 1) What is the "extdata" used in the Vignette? I did not use it to create "file.list" (even though specified in the Vignette, because I would get an error), but I did use it to create "gene.obj".
>

   extdata directory is in the  installation folder and contains example data. You should not need that for your own data.  Just location of your files. Check the examples and and type "file.list" in R console, you will see it just contains paths to files.

> 2) How is the "refseq.hg18.bed.txt" different than "hg18" in the vignette? What is the .bed.txt file? I have the reference genome "refpdom.fasta", which I used to create "myobj", but I do not know whether or how to create the .bed.txt file (which is why I am not surprised about this error).

BED file is a tabular text file contains the locations of genomic features (chr,start,end,strand, etc.). You seem to just have a fasta file which contains the sequences of transcripts possibly.
 See this post and click the links there to know more about BED format and how to download it. I don't know if you can download it for your species of interest.
http://zvfak.blogspot.ch/2012/09/downloading-annotation-files-for.html

> 3) Is it problematic that my control and variable information is of different length? For instance, my two input files are "queenDataHasC.txt" and "workerDataHasC.txt". One file is 2,521,760 lines long, the other is 2,674,819 lines long. (They were originally 58,828,763 and 57,901,315 lines long. However, for each file, I removed lines with freqC = 0).
>

It is not a problem if you are aware of the fact that you can not compare regions/bases that are not covered in one of the samples (if you have one control and one test sample). If you have removed the lines with freqC=0, then it also explains why you don't have bimodal distribution. You removed everything that has zero methylation (I guess that was intentional?).

messages.body_plain:
Yes, you can download the Ensembl genes in the same manner as described for Refseq in the webpage, It should have the same information but with different chromosome naming convetion, it will have "chr" string in front of numbers.

However, the particular problem here is that somewhat related to R, also related to how I coded the methylKit to read files faster. The code reads first 100 lines of a text file and decides what would be the column type (numeric or factor/character) and reads the rest of the file with that expectation. Your files has chromosome numbers instead of "chr"+number so the code expects that column would be numeric but encounters a string and throws an error. There are two ways to deal with this:

1) I think if you append "chr" string in the first column it would work. If you have number for chromosomes in SAM file or methylation percentage file instead of the "chr"+number version, it is best you do the same for them as well to avoid downstream problems because of different chromosome naming conventions . You can do this with awk or something like that with a one liner.
2) put that problematic line as the first line of the file, so the function knows that there are strings in that column, and assigns the appropriate type for the column.

Best,
Altuna

messages.subject: Re: Question about methylKit
messages.body_plain:
Hello:

Altuna and I discussed 6-bed format versus 12-bed format, and I am posting the solution I used to get the 12-bed format directly from .gff3 file.

I used the Galaxy link (https://galaxy.cbio.mskcc.org/tool_runner?tool_id=fml_gff2bed). This converts .gff3 to 12-bed format. You must first upload your .gff3 dataset to the history (https://usegalaxy.org/). Then when you go to the link (https://galaxy.cbio.mskcc.org/tool_runner?tool_id=fml_gff2bed), the .gff3 file should be available, and just click "Execute" to convert to 12-column .bed file.

You can expect the number of lines in the files to reduce from .gff3 to 12-bed format.

An explanation from Jen of Galaxy is as follows:

"A reduction in the number of lines is completely expected. You should have the same number of lines in the BED12 file as you have unique "ID"s in the GFF3 file, if you want to double check. This is the same as the number of unique transcripts in any of the files, if summed up correctly.

Why is this? A GFF3 file has one line per feature. Part of an exon, etc. with further (this can vary) annotation that tells you if it is 5' UTR, or CDS, etc. When converting GFF3 -> BED12, all the features for a particular transcript are rolled up into a single line of output. Transcripts will have a unique "ID" by GFF3 specification - and all features that belong to that transcript will have it in the GFF3 file's attributes field (it is usually the first attribute listed).

When you converted just GFF3 -> BED6, each feature was individually converted into a distinct line of BED formatted output, there was no summing up to group the information for the transcript as a whole. "
Thank you!

L. Rutter

On Thursday, November 7, 2013 9:00:18 PM UTC+11, Altuna Akalin wrote:
> do:
> myobj[[2][ is.na <http://is.na>(myobj[[2]]$numCs/myobj[[2]]$coverage),]
>
> and check those rows that generate NA/NaN values. The problem might be that maybe NA character is not recognised by R, maybe they are using a different one. Or maybe, there is a division by 0 creates NaN values. In any case, the code above gets you the rows that are problematic. And you can figure out what to do from there on. If NaN values are created, somehow coverage 0 bases are in your file. Check if you are using the correct column from BSMAP output. If there are other NA characters that you are not filtering for, filter them as well.
>
> Best,
> Altuna
>

Thanks Altuna,

Turned out using Bsmap I had some C's with an effective coverage of 0.5 and below.  Removing these lines sorted out the issues

Ian.

In that case I would need suggestions from other about which tool would be better to use with whole genome bisulfite sequencing data for plants.

You can try to use it. Although I have never done it, some users managed to use methylKit with whole-genome BS. You might need a high-memory machine as all the methylation data will be read-in and kept in memory. I do not know any other tools in R that will not suffer from this. You can also try to process the data chromosome by chromsome if memory requirement becomes a problem. There might be something outside of R/Bioconductor world that maybe more memory efficient, but I don't know about those.

> Our collaborator has generated two sets of files one with all c positions in the genome annotating them to be methylated or unmethlyated and one with only the positions that were methylated. This might seem like a stupid question but in your opinion which file should I rely on to use for the analysis.
>

I'm not sure that's the right format. You need coverage information and number of methylated and unmethylated calls per C. The format you are describing sounds like a binary format. Have a look at the vignette and the webpage to see examples of the format. Assuming you have the right format, some people will only be interested in CpG methylation, in plants methylation in other contexts are probably also important (CHG and CHH) so you would probably want a file that have methylation information on all Cs. But as I said, it depends what your collaborators are interested in.

Best,
Altuna

messages.subject: Filter by coverage after destrand
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am trying to use the MethylKit package to analyse my case-control cohort of RRBS libraries, and have encountered a problem.

Ideally, I would like to use the destrand=TRUE function to allow the read coverage on forward and reverse strand of a given CpG dinucleotide to be merged. However, I would also like to filter by coverage - i.e. require at least 10 reads at a given CpG locus. The filtering tools available however, perform this filtering before the merging of CpG dinucleotides, so that in essence one requires at least 10 reads on one, the other or both the forward and reverse strands. This means that a large amount of data ends up being discarded when, for instance one has 9 reads on each strand - totalling 18 at a CpG site. Under the current filtering, this entire site would be discarded, although all together it meets the filtering requirements. Likewise, if one has 20 reads on one strand, and 7 on the other, only the 20 of those reads that are on the strand that meets filtering requirements would be analysed.

Do you have any advice for resolving this problem?
>From what I can tell, the filterByCoverage function won't run on a methylBase object such as is produced by the unite function

I haven't managed to find any documentation, but perhaps I am looking in the wrong places?

I look forward to hearing your thoughts

Thanks

Hester Roberts

Hi Altuna,

I am a colleague of Cindy and investigated her issue more in depth.
I found that because we are working with rather short scaffolds, our g.meth object within regionalize.R (tileMethylCounts) contains more seqname levels than there actually are. This will then cause regionCounts to be executed on chromosomes which do not exist, resulting in empty data.frames and thus NA errors.

The quickfix for our error is to replace line 336 in regionalize.R:
chrs   =IRanges::levels(seqnames(g.meth))
 by
chrs   =unique(seqnames(g.meth))

I am no expert in the GenomicRanges package, but maybe there is also a function to drop the empty seqnames from the levels?
I hope this provides you some more insight into our error. Would you please care to update us if this is something which would be changed in a new version of the package or not?

Evelyne
